opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think 2025 is going to be a really interesting year, and if I had to sum it up in one phrase, it would be "the year agents start to actually work."

Over the past two years, most of the excitement was about large language models as chatbots: you ask a question, it gives you an answer. That's already very useful, but it's still fundamentally a passive interaction. What changed toward the end of 2024, with reasoning models like OpenAI's o1 and the open-source efforts that followed, is that we now have models that can think for a long time, reflect, correct themselves, and plan over multiple steps. Once a model can reason like that, the natural next step is to let it *act*: browse the web, write and run code, operate software, call tools, and complete a task end to end rather than just producing text.

From my perspective as someone who works on reinforcement learning, this is very exciting, because the key technology behind it is RL. Pretraining gives you a model that knows a lot, but RL is what teaches it to pursue a goal, try things, fail, and learn from feedback. I think in 2025 we'll see RL move from a niche research topic to a core part of how frontier models are built. A lot of the competition will shift from "who has the biggest pretraining run" to "who has the best RL infrastructure, the best environments, and the best reward signals."

On applications, I'd point to a few directions. First, coding agents. Code is an ideal domain because the feedback is verifiable: the program runs or it doesn't, and tests pass or they don't. I expect coding assistants to evolve from autocomplete into something closer to a junior engineer that can take an issue and deliver a working change. Second, research and information agents, the "deep research" type of product, where the model spends minutes or even hours gathering and synthesizing information for you. Third, more general computer-use agents that operate a browser or a desktop. Those are harder and will still be pretty rough in 2025, but I think we'll see real progress.

I'd also add a note of caution. Agents are much harder to make reliable than chatbots. If a chatbot is wrong 10% of the time, you just ask again. If an agent executing a 20-step task has a small error rate at each step, the whole task fails very often. So a lot of the work in 2025 will be quite unglamorous: building better environments, better evaluation, and better systems for training at scale. The demos will look amazing, but the gap between a demo and a product people rely on every day is still real.

And finally, I'm quite optimistic about the open-source community, especially in China. We've seen that teams with fewer resources can still do very competitive work through smart algorithms and good engineering. So I think 2025 won't just be a story about one or two big labs. There will be a lot of room for academia and smaller teams to contribute, particularly on the RL and agent side, where good ideas still matter enormously.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame 2025 with one word: agents. But let me be careful about what I mean by that, because the word gets thrown around a lot.

For the past two years the dominant interaction with AI has been conversational. You ask, it answers. That's a chat paradigm, and it's been incredibly valuable, but it's fundamentally a tool you hold in your hand. What's changing in 2025 is that the model stops being an answer machine and starts being something that can plan, act over multiple steps, call tools, check its own work, and recover from mistakes. That's a different kind of artifact. In my own research, coming from reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems, this is the part that excites me most, because it's finally where the "decision-making" side of AI and the "language" side of AI merge.

Technically, there are three threads I'd watch.

First, reasoning. The shift toward models that spend more compute at inference time, that think before they answer, is real and it's not a gimmick. The interesting part isn't that benchmarks go up. It's that this kind of capability is trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes, which means the recipe generalizes to any domain where you can check whether the answer is right. Code, math, and increasingly things like scientific analysis. In 2025 I expect that recipe to get much cheaper and much more widespread, including from Chinese teams. I'd actually say the gap in this area is narrower than most people assume.

Second, the price of intelligence collapsing. A year ago, capability at the frontier cost a lot per token. Now you can get last year's frontier for a tiny fraction of the price. That matters more for applications than any single new model does, because it changes what you can afford to do. You can afford to let the model try ten times, let it reflect, let it run in the background for an hour. A lot of agent designs that were economically impossible become reasonable.

Third, multimodality and embodiment, but I'd put a slower clock on those. Video understanding and generation will keep improving. Robotics will see impressive demos. But the data problem for the physical world is much harder than for text, and I don't think 2025 is the year it crosses into broad deployment.

On applications, my honest view is that the first wave of "AI native" apps mostly didn't work, because they were thin wrappers around a chat box. The second wave that I think succeeds looks less like a chatbot and more like a coworker in a specific vertical: coding is the obvious one and already happening, then customer service, research assistance, data analysis, and certain enterprise workflows where the task is well-defined and the output is checkable. The products that win won't be the ones with the best model. They'll be the ones that figured out the evaluation loop: how to tell when the agent is right, how to let a human intervene cheaply, how to build trust incrementally.

I'd add a word of caution. Agents amplify both capability and error. An assistant that answers wrongly wastes thirty seconds. An agent that acts wrongly can waste a day or break something. So reliability, not raw intelligence, is going to be the bottleneck for adoption. The teams that treat this as an engineering and training problem, rather than hoping the next model solves it, will be the ones that actually ship.

So, optimistic, but in a specific way. 2025 isn't the year of some dramatic new capability appearing out of nowhere. It's the year the capabilities we already have become cheap enough and reliable enough to be put to work.

astra-6.text:
I think 2025 could be a year when the focus shifts from what AI can demonstrate to what people can reliably use it for. The exciting question is whether it can help someone complete a meaningful task, with less effort and at a reasonable cost.

One direction I’m particularly interested in is AI moving from answering questions to carrying out tasks. For example, an assistant might help you organize information, develop a plan, and work through several steps with your feedback. That opens up possibilities in programming, education, research, and everyday office work.

But there’s a gap between a convincing demonstration and a dependable application. If a system performs well most of the time but makes errors that are difficult to notice, users still have to spend considerable effort checking it. So reliability, cost, and knowing when to ask for human help will matter as much as raw capability.

Overall, I’m optimistic, but I expect progress to be uneven. Some narrowly defined applications may become useful quite quickly. More general assistants will need time. The strongest products will probably start with a clear user need and show that AI actually makes the task easier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think 2025 will be a year when AI moves further from impressive demonstrations into practical applications. The key question will be whether it can reliably complete useful tasks at a cost people can afford.

One area I’m watching is AI agents: systems that can use tools, work through several steps, and help people finish a task. There’s a big difference between answering a question and handling a workflow, though. Reliability becomes much more important when a system takes action, so I expect progress first in well-defined tasks where people can check the results.

We’ll also see more applications that combine text, images, and voice. That could make AI much easier to use in education, software development, and everyday work. But adoption will depend on more than model capability. Products need to fit how people actually work, protect their data, and deliver clear value.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t expect every industry to change overnight. The strongest applications will solve specific problems well, and broader changes will grow from that.
